speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ballast water is water that is taken on board ships to provide balance and stability to ships.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The discharge of ballast water from ships is one of the principal ways potentially invasive alien marine species are introduced into marine environments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The environmental and economic damage caused by invasive species can be substantial.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Convention seeks to prevent the transfer of harmful marine species and pathogens from one marine environment to another.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is done by establishing standards and procedures for the management of ships' ballast water and sediments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Convention places restrictions on the uptake and discharge of ballast water by ships and mandates the safe disposal of sediments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It was adopted by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) in February 2004 and will be entering into force in September 2017.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The proposed Prevention of Pollution of the Sea (Amendment) Bill 2017 enables Singapore to comply with the Convention.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Louis Ng has also separately mentioned to me just now that he supports the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: He also shared some feedback on the penalties and exemptions in the Bill which I will talk about shortly.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Clause 6 prohibits the discharge of sediments into Singapore waters, from any place on land, or from any apparatus used for transferring sediments from or to any ship.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Clause 9 prohibits the discharge of untreated ballast water or sediments into Singapore waters from any ship, or from a Singapore ship into any sea.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Clause 9 also empowers the Maritime and Port Authority (MPA) to make regulations to exempt ships from the prohibition against discharge of ballast water and sediments into our waters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked me about how and when such exemptions will be given.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: One possible exemption could be for ships that operate exclusively within a specified area, if the risk of transfer of invasive species through the discharge of their ballast water is deemed acceptable based on IMO's risk assessment guidelines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Clauses 5, 7 and 8 revise the penalties for the discharge of pollutants, garbage and noxious liquid substances into our waters.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The increase in fines ensures that the financial penalty continues to serve as an effective deterrent against pollution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The reduced jail term avoids unduly penalising seafarers for pollution-related offences committed during their course of work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In this aspect, MPA's experience has been that pollution-related offences are more often a result of shipboard conditions arising from the actions of the employers, than that it is due to individual seafarers acting on their own accord.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Clause 10 increases the financial penalty limits for contraventions of regulations relating to the provision of reception facilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The maximum jail term has also been retained.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Under the Convention, terminals, including shipyards, that provide ballast tank repair, cleaning or retrofitting services, should provide for the reception of sediments from ships.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The higher penalties that may be levied on reception facilities reflect the severity of the damage to the environment that their contraventions may cause.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Clause 11 empowers MPA to make regulations requiring Singapore-flagged ships and ships in Singapore waters to carry ballast water record books on board.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Clause 13 imposes a duty on land occupiers or persons in charge of apparatus for transferring sediments from which sediments have been discharged into Singapore waters, to report such discharge.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Clause 16 amends section 34 of the Act to empower MPA, with the approval of the Minister, to make regulations to give effect to the Convention.

speaker: The Second Minister for Transport (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The shipping industry has been consulted and they are supportive of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ships have been using sea water as a ballast to stabilise ships at sea for more than a hundred years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sea water is pumped into or out of ships to achieve safe and desirable operating conditions for the ships.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It helps the ships to maintain stability and enhances manoeuvrability, especially when the sea conditions or the volume of cargo, fuel or water onboard a ship may change in the course of each voyage.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Stress on the ship's hull may also be reduced accordingly with the use of ballast water.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A ship may take in seawater for ballast at a particular location and discharge the same water at a different part of the world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What this means is that the ship will unwittingly transport all micro-organisms and marine species in the sea water from one part of the world to another part of the world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such species may include microbes, bacteria, small invertebrates, larvae, eggs and cysts of different species.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Frequently, some of such species may survive and reproduce in the new environment where they have been discharged, compete with the local species and becoming effectively pests in the new environment and affecting the new environment in an adverse way.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ballast Water Convention introduces global regulations to control the transfer of potentially invasive species.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under the Ballast Water Convention, all ships must install appropriate ballast water treatment systems.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ships must have a ballast water record book, recording the occasions when ballast water is taken onboard or treated for ballast water management purposes, discharged into a reception facility as well as any accidental discharges of ballast water.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The aim is to prevent, minimise and, ultimately, eliminate the transfer of harmful organisms and pathogens through the control and management of ships ballast water sediments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As Singapore is one of the busiest ports in the world and sits by one of the busiest sea channels in the world, we have many vessels coming into our port waters or passaging through nearby seas.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The risk of invasive species causing ecological damage to our seas and marine environment cannot be discounted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another reason that I support this Bill is because Singapore is among one of the top five ship registries in the world and has over 4,000 ships under its registry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The operation of our system, our Singapore flagship, does not affect only our Singapore waters but also affects the seas around the world as the vessels ply the international waters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has taken a while for Singapore to introduce the Ballast Water Convention into our legislation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Convention came up way back in 2004.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But given the environmental concerns we have heard and given the fact that we are one of the busiest ports in the world, one of the five largest ship registries in the world and one of the leading maritime hubs in the world, if the Government is of the view that such convention is the right way forward, then perhaps we should have ratified the Convention earlier.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In contrast, by way of examples, countries like Malaysia ratified the Convention in 2010 and Australia and Indonesia in 2016.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked about the adequacy of penalties and whether Singapore should have acceded to the Ballast Water Management Convention earlier.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: I have spoken earlier about the penalties set out in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: But let me add that we recognise that ballast water discharges can have a significant impact on the environment.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: As such, the proposed penalties are commensurate with other existing environmental pollution-related offences.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: So, the whole set of laws is aligned and the professionals have said that these are adequate.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: We can always monitor and see whether they are an adequate deterrent.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: On whether Singapore should have acceded to the Convention earlier, let me explain our considerations.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Singapore takes the protection of marine environment very seriously.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: We have ratified every major IMO Convention relating to the prevention of pollution from ships, including the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: Hence, rather than rush into acceding to this Convention, Singapore has been working with IMO and the industry to address outstanding implementation issues that the industry has raised.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: One of the main concerns has been that the IMO's guidelines for approving ballast water management systems were not rigorous enough, such that approved systems did not consistently meet the Convention's standards for discharged ballast water.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng
text: This Bill seeks to enable us to fulfil our obligations under the Convention and continue to keep our flag flying high.
